transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-25 14:30 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Leah (Redwood SRE), Priya (Synapse CTO), Rajiv (Platform), Samira (ML), Tom (Infra)

Summary: Deep dive into intermittent GPU OOM spikes seen on Synapse's dedicated cluster during variable-length LLM workloads. Focus on CUDA context eviction, KV cache interactions with batching, and retry semantics that surface timeouts. Actionable tasks: capture nvlog/dmesg, enable driver-level tracing for next run, introduce conservative batching and kernel hysteresis, and tweak retry backoff.

00:00:05 Maya (Redwood): Hey all, thanks for taking the time, we'll keep this focused on the OOMs + timeouts you reported, and walk through the repro, traces, and potential mitigations.
00:00:12 Priya (Synapse): Yeah thanks Maya. We've had a couple of incidents last week where a handful of inference requests caused whole GPU pods to go into OOM and then they cascade to other tenants. Not sure if it's kv cache or the batching windows.
00:00:28 Daniel (Redwood SE): Quick ask before we dig in — can you confirm the driver and CUDA versions? And are you on multi-instance MPS or one process per GPU?
00:00:36 Tom (Synapse Infra): We're on NV driver 525.89 (ish), CUDA 11.8, and we run one process per GPU with our own containerized scheduler. No MPS.
00:00:45 Leah (Redwood SRE): Noted — one process per GPU simplifies some things but also means eviction looks like a full OOM rather than context preemption.

00:01:12 Samira (ML): The pattern we see: long prompt streams with many short completions, sometimes we have prefix-KV hits (cache) but when sequence length suddenly jumps (user paste large context) we spike and then the pod dies with kernel oops on dmesg.
00:01:30 Daniel: That screams sequence-length variance + batching. If the runtime batches across requests with different seq lengths without proper memory headroom, the peak can blow out. Couple that with KV cache pinned allocations and you get fragmentation + sudden allocation failure.

00:02:05 Rajiv: We have logs — attached to the ticket — showing repeated cudaMalloc failures then driver messages: "GPU OOM: failed to allocate 6.1 GiB" and then a process killed by oom-killer. We do also see context timeout entries around the same time.
00:02:22 Daniel: Two axes to consider: 1) transient fragmentation/allocator behavior inside the runtime (cudaMalloc vs caching allocators like CUB/THC) and 2) external evictions/timeouts from the driver when kernel runtime exceeds watchdog or PCIe stalls. The logs you sent show both.

00:03:01 Maya: Let's step through the repro you ran. Rajiv, can you describe the workload shape and batching config?
00:03:08 Rajiv: We use dynamic batching with max_batch_size=16, batch_timeout_ms=50, and a prefix KV cache enabled for repeat trivias. Typical seq lengths 64-256, but occasionally a 2048 or 4096 arrives. We had quantized 8-bit for the 30B variant.
00:03:29 Daniel: There it is — mixed quantization + large seq spikes + batching. Quantized kernels may use different scratch buffer sizes; when the runtime switches kernels (quantized->fp16 fallback for certain ops) we can allocate additional temporaries. If your kernel selection logic isn't conservative, allocations happen mid-inference and push you over the edge.

00:04:02 Priya: We also saw one case where the first few requests in a pod were fine, then after ~6 hours we started to see failures even for smaller seq lengths. Could that be memory leak or fragmentation?
00:04:14 Leah: Yes, fragmentation or memory not being returned to the device allocator is a possibility. Also if KV cache entries grow over time because of unexpected prefix retention, that raises resident usage. We recommend periodic KV eviction or an LRU cap per model shard.

00:04:45 Daniel: A few concrete things we want you to collect next run: nvprof/nvtx trace, the runtime allocator histogram (we'll share a collector), dmesg + /var/log/messages around the time, and the model's KV cache metadata (count and sizes). We'll provide a checklist.

00:05:10 Rajiv: We can run that tomorrow. Curious — are there known issues with the driver version you mentioned?
00:05:16 Daniel: Drivers in the 525-530 range had some reported timeout regression with long-running kernels and certain PCIe sequences. Also CUDA 11.8's allocator semantics changed; depending on the allocator (jemalloc vs cuda's pool) fragmentation patterns change. We can put a note in the checklist about trying a repro with 535.x or the vendor-suggested stable driver.

00:06:02 Samira: Could batching policy be adapted so that when a large seq arrives we don't force the whole batch to allocate for max length?
00:06:12 Daniel: Yes — two strategies: 1) bucketed batching by sequence length (small/medium/large) so similar-length requests are batched; 2) dynamic micro-batching with per-request allocation caps, i.e., pre-validate memory headroom and reject or defer large requests. Bucketed batching usually reduces worst-case peaks.

00:06:48 Maya: Also worth mentioning the runtime supports kernel hysteresis — we can delay switching to a larger-kernel implementation until a moving-average of requests exceeds a threshold. That avoids frequent kernel flapping which creates alloc churn.

00:07:10 Tom: We run in a VPC/private env, so we don't want any external calls. Any debug flags safe for production?
00:07:18 Daniel: We have a low-overhead tracing mode that records allocator events and nvtx markers locally; it writes to ephemeral storage and can be rotated. It's safe but we need to watch disk if you enable it cluster-wide. We'll provide the config patch to enable in staging.

00:07:49 Rajiv: About retries — we have a client-side retry that retries on 502/timeout with fixed backoff. That sometimes amplifies load when a pod is flapping.
00:07:58 Leah: Fixed backoff is dangerous here. Recommend exponential backoff with jitter and a max retry cap. Also a 'circuit-breaker' at the router level to avoid retry storms — if a node reports OOM within last X minutes, route to another node or degrade to a smaller model.

00:08:30 Samira: What about quantization fallbacks? We saw a fallback to fp16 for some attention ops which increased memory usage. Can the runtime avoid fallback if it triggers OOMs?
00:08:42 Daniel: Two levers: explict quantization profiles that mark ops as 'must-stay-quantized' (with possible accuracy cost), or a soft-fallback that tries smaller batch sizes instead of changing kernel type. We can add a safety check: if fallback would increase resident memory beyond threshold, prefer batching change.

00:09:20 Priya: Any quick wins we can try today?
00:09:24 Maya: Yes: 1) Reduce max_batch_size to 8 or lower as a temporary mitigation, 2) enable sequence bucketing, 3) set a strict per-request seq-length limit (reject > 1024 unless explicit reserve), and 4) enable exponential retry backoff on the client side.

00:09:45 Rajiv: We'll try batch size 8 and sequence cap.

00:10:02 Daniel: Longer term: we recommend enabling the runtime's allocator pool tuning, configure KV cache LRU caps per model shard, and add kernel hysteresis parameters. We'll draft PRs for those configs.

00:10:25 Tom: One more oddity — sometimes we see kernel hang and driver reports a PCIe error before OOM. Could that be thermal or hardware?
00:10:36 Leah: Yes PCIe stalls and thermal throttling can manifest similarly. Check GPU temps and ECC logs. Also check system-level preemption settings; sometimes long-running kernels get preempted in ways that leave the process in a bad state. We'll include thermal checks in the checklist.

00:11:10 Priya: What's the suggested retry policy code snippet?
00:11:15 Daniel: We'll send a one-liner: exponential backoff with jitter, max retries 3, and a client-visible hint to the router to avoid immediate reroute to same pod. We'll paste that in the follow-up.

00:11:40 Maya: Let's look at the specific log from 2026-04-18 incident (Rajiv uploaded).
00:11:47 (screen share)
00:11:50 Rajiv: Key lines: "malloc returned NULL" then "[drm] GPU hung: recovery start" then several "context destroyed" messages. The runtimes' allocator shows many small frees but not large contiguous free region.
00:12:10 Daniel: Fragmentation. If malloc returns NULL despite total free memory being high, it's a sign of fragmented address space. Two mitigations: 1) use pooled allocators / defragmenter (we have experimental heap compaction routines), 2) avoid frequent alloc/dealloc of large temporaries by reusing a scratch arena per model copy.

00:13:05 Samira: Is it feasible to pin the KV cache in host memory instead of device?
00:13:12 Daniel: Yes — host-pinned KV is a valid trade-off: higher latency but lower device resident usage. You can move less-frequently-used KV segments to host and keep hot ones device-resident. We can help you instrument access patterns to decide cutover policy.

00:13:45 Priya: Any security/compliance caveats when we enable tracing? We have strict audit needs.
00:13:52 Maya: Traces are kept internal and can be stored in your S3 with KMS. We also have filtered traces that redact tokens. We'll provide the redaction config.

00:14:20 Daniel: Another angle — when a pod OOMs, our rollout policy can spin a warm replica with a warm KV snapshot so warm-up allocation doesn't spike. Warm pre-warming avoids the first-request alloc storm.
00:14:38 Rajiv: How expensive is pre-warming memory?
00:14:42 Daniel: It costs GPU cycles and some time — but you can keep a small pool of warm standbys. There's also an on-demand warm path that streams allocations in background while serving light requests. We'll include recommended sizes in the checklist.

00:15:10 Priya: Let's capture decisions: we'll do immediate mitigations (reduce batch size, seq cap, exponential backoff), collect traces next run, and plan follow-up to implement allocator/kv changes.
00:15:22 Maya: Yes. We'll queue up the driver test with 535.x in staging. Also we'll propose kernel hysteresis and pooling PRs.

00:15:45 (rest of call — technical deep dive continues with Daniel walking through stack traces, code pointers, and config snippets; timestamps omitted for brevity)

Approximately 50m of detailed walkthrough with code references, suggested config patches, and discussion of edge-case: multi-tenant contention where one heavy batch starves allocator and causes eviction of other model contexts. Discussed circuit-breaker strategies and telemetry alerts (high alloc failure rate => auto-scale or throttle).

Closing (last 2 minutes)
00:58:40 Maya: Recap — action items in Fireflies and I'll send the perf triage template and the safe trace flags. Daniel will draft the kernel hysteresis proposal and Leah will add retry backoff in staging.
00:59:02 Priya: Thanks everyone, this was super useful. We'll run the capture and get logs over to you.
00:59:15 Maya: Great — we'll sync next week.

Notes/links shared during call: https://redwood-internal.example.com/perf-triage-checklist (secure link), ticket #SF-4421, sample dmesg excerpt (attached in CRM).
